clinicalScope: Gilbert syndrome in adult patients in low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Gilbert Syndrome
subject: Pathology
summary: A benign, autosomal‑recessive disorder of bilirubin conjugation causing mild, episodic unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. It worsens with fasting, infection or stress and is usually asymptomatic.

sections.p: Gilbert syndrome is a mild, inherited defect in UDP‑glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) activity, leading to impaired conjugation of bilirubin.

t.b: Suggests Gilbert syndrome when other causes excluded

t.a: Liver function tests (AST, ALT, ALP, GGT)

sections.p: Severity is graded by peak bilirubin levels and frequency of jaundice episodes.
The primary defect is reduced UGT1A1 activity due to a promoter mutation.

t.b: Not routinely available in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Patients are usually asymptomatic; jaundice appears during fasting, infection, strenuous exercise or pregnancy.
b: Sudden yellowing of sclera and skin

sections.p: Investigations aim to exclude other causes of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
b: CBC with reticulocyte count – rules out haemolysis
Peripheral smear – looks for spherocytes or schistocytes

t.b: Elevated unconjugated with normal direct suggests Gilbert

sections.p: Complications are rare but include severe jaundice during pregnancy or prolonged fasting.
b: Severe hyperbilirubinaemia (>10 mg/dL) can cause kernicterus in neonates

sections.p: No specific treatment is required; focus is on reassurance and avoiding precipitating factors.
b: Advise regular meals, avoid prolonged fasting

t.b: Avoid in pregnancy and low‑resource settings

sections.p: Regular follow‑up is usually unnecessary; counsel patients on lifestyle.

whenToSeekHelp: Jaundice with abdominal pain or dark urine

faq.q: Can Gilbert syndrome cause liver damage?
faq.a: No, it is a benign disorder with normal liver enzymes.

exam: What is the most likely cause of mild, episodic jaundice in a 28‑year‑old man with normal liver enzymes? — Reduced UGT1A1 activity (Gilbert syndrome).
Which investigation would best rule out haemolysis in this patient? — Reticulocyte count and peripheral smear.
A patient with Gilbert syndrome develops severe jaundice during pregnancy. What is the most appropriate management? — Reassurance, avoid fasting, monitor bilirubin, consider phototherapy if newborn.
Why is phenobarbital not routinely used in low‑resource settings for Gilbert syndrome? — It induces UGT1A1 but has limited availability and potential side effects.
What laboratory finding would distinguish Gilbert syndrome from Crigler‑Najjar syndrome? — In Crigler‑Najjar, bilirubin >20 mg/dL with no response to phenobarbital.
A patient presents with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and a history of malaria. Which condition must be excluded first? — Hemolytic anaemia secondary to malaria.
